lines.title: BITS AND QUBITS
lines.text: An ordinary bit is always either zero or one. A qubit can be in a combination of both until it is measured. This combination is called a superposition. The glowing arrow shows the state of one qubit.

lines.title: KET ZERO
lines.text: Right now the arrow points straight up, at |0⟩. To find out what a qubit holds, we measure it. A measurement gives one of just two answers: zero or one. At |0⟩, it gives zero every time. Next, the arrow is turned all the way down.

lines.title: KET ONE
lines.text: Straight down is |1⟩. Here a measurement gives one every time. The very top and the very bottom are the only places where the answer is certain.

lines.title: IN BETWEEN
lines.text: Anywhere between the top and the bottom, the qubit is in a superposition. A measurement can then give either answer, and which one you get is a matter of chance. The higher the tip, the more often you get zero. Exactly halfway down, zero and one are equally likely.

lines.title: THE THREE AXES
lines.text: The sphere has three axes. The z axis runs up and down, from |0⟩ to |1⟩. The x and y axes lie flat across the middle. The circle around the middle of the sphere is called the equator.

lines.title: ON THE EQUATOR
lines.text: Four points on the equator have names. Along x are |+⟩ and |−⟩. Along y are |+i⟩ and |−i⟩.

lines.title: AROUND THE EQUATOR
lines.text: The arrow is now at |+⟩. Next, it moves around the equator a quarter turn at a time, through the other three named states. Watch its height as it goes.

lines.title: SAME HEIGHT, SAME ODDS
lines.text: That was |+i⟩, |−⟩, and |−i⟩. The height never changed, so every one of these states gives zero half the time. A measurement cannot tell them apart. So what makes them different states? Keep that question in mind.

lines.title: YOUR TURN TO PREDICT
lines.text: After each part of this lesson there is a short exercise. The arrow is back at |0⟩. Next, it gets a quarter turn toward |1⟩.

lines.title: GATES
lines.text: Every change to a qubit, short of measuring it, is a turn of the arrow about an axis. A fixed turn that quantum computers use again and again is called a gate. The arrow is at |+⟩, where the exercise left it.

lines.title: THE Z GATE
lines.text: The Z gate is a half turn about the z axis. Next, Z is applied to |+⟩.

lines.title: WHAT Z DID
lines.text: Z swung the arrow halfway around the equator, to |−⟩. Its height did not change, so the odds did not change either: |−⟩ still gives zero half the time. Z changed something real that a measurement cannot see. This direction around the equator is the phase.

lines.title: TURN DIRECTION
lines.text: Every turn has a direction. Point the thumb of your right hand along the axis. Your fingers curl the way the arrow turns. For the z axis, with your thumb pointing up, that is counterclockwise when seen from above.

lines.title: THE S GATE
lines.text: The S gate is a quarter turn about the z axis. Next, S is applied to |+⟩. Use your right hand: where will it land?

lines.title: WHAT S DID
lines.text: S took |+⟩ a quarter turn counterclockwise, to |+i⟩. Like Z, it changed only the phase. The height, and so the odds, stayed the same.

lines.title: THE X GATE
lines.text: Not every gate turns about z. The X gate is a half turn about the x axis. The arrow is at |0⟩. Next, X is applied.

lines.title: WHAT X DID
lines.text: X took |0⟩ at the top to |1⟩ at the bottom. This time the height changed, so the odds changed too: from always zero to always one. X flips a qubit, just like flipping an ordinary bit.

lines.title: THE Y GATE
lines.text: The Y gate is a half turn about the y axis. It also flips the arrow, but about a different axis. Next, Y is applied to |1⟩.

lines.title: THE H GATE
lines.text: The arrow is back at |0⟩. The H gate is named after the mathematician Hadamard. It is a half turn about a tilted axis, halfway between the x axis and the z axis. Next, H is applied to |0⟩.

lines.title: WHAT H DID
lines.text: H took |0⟩ from the top down to |+⟩ on the equator: from a certain answer to an equal superposition. Z and S only move the arrow around the equator. H can move it between top and equator. Next, S is applied.

lines.title: WHAT COMES NEXT
lines.text: S took |+⟩ to |+i⟩. For the exercise, the arrow will get one more S.

lines.title: UNDOING GATES
lines.text: Every gate is a turn, so every gate can be undone by turning back. The arrow is at |0⟩. Next, it gets two X gates in a row.

lines.title: X UNDOES X
lines.text: Two half turns about the same axis make one full turn, so the second X undid the first.

lines.title: FOUR S GATES
lines.text: The arrow is at |+⟩. Next, it gets four S gates in a row.

lines.title: FOUR QUARTER TURNS
lines.text: Four quarter turns make a full turn, so the arrow is back at |+⟩. Along the way, two S gates did the same job as one Z: a half turn about z.

lines.title: H TWICE
lines.text: The arrow is at |0⟩. Next, it gets H twice.

lines.title: H UNDOES ITSELF
lines.text: H, then H again, brings |0⟩ back to |0⟩. Now back to the question from Part 1. Next, |0⟩ gets an H again, but this time a Z follows.

lines.title: WHAT COMES NEXT
lines.text: The arrow is at |−⟩. As far as a measurement can tell, nothing changed: |+⟩ and |−⟩ both give zero half the time. Next, H is applied again, just as before.

lines.title: WHAT JUST HAPPENED
lines.text: H then H brought |0⟩ back to |0⟩. H, Z, H landed on |1⟩, the opposite answer. The only difference was a Z, which on its own changed nothing a measurement could see. H turned that hidden phase into height. This is called interference, and quantum algorithms are built on it. It is also why a qubit needs complex numbers: they carry the phase.

lines.title: MEASUREMENT
lines.text: Now a closer look at measurement. A measurement gives zero or one, and it also changes the qubit. Right after, the arrow points straight at the answer you got: up for zero, down for one.

lines.title: SETTING UP
lines.text: The arrow is at |0⟩. Next, it gets an H.

lines.title: ONE RESULT IS NOT ENOUGH
lines.text: The arrow is at |+⟩, on the equator. Measuring it once gives a single zero or a single one, which tells us very little. So the same state is prepared again and again, and measured each time. The panel counts the results.

lines.title: ONE HUNDRED RESULTS
lines.text: About half gave zero and half gave one. Each single result is chance, but over many measurements the counts follow the state.

lines.title: THE HEIGHT RULE
lines.text:
Read the height of the tip on a scale from minus one at the bottom to plus one at the top. The chance of zero is one plus the height, divided by two. At the top, that is one hundred percent. On the equator, fifty. At the bottom, zero.

<align=center><size=130%>P(0) = (1 + height) / 2</size></align>

lines.title: HEIGHT, NOT ANGLE
lines.text: The chance follows the height of the tip, not how far the arrow has turned. Near the top, a turn barely changes the height. Near the equator, the same turn changes it a lot. This chance is |α|² from the start of the lesson.

lines.title: MEASURING AGAIN
lines.text: Measuring again right away gives the same answer every time, because the arrow already points at it. And unlike a gate, a measurement cannot be undone by turning back.

lines.title: WHAT A MEASUREMENT SEES
lines.text: A measurement only reads height. So it always tells apart opposite points at the top and bottom, like |0⟩ and |1⟩. Ket plus and |−⟩ are opposite too, but at the same height. That is why, in Part 3, an H was needed to tell them apart.

lines.title: WHAT COMES NEXT
lines.text: The arrow is back at |0⟩. Next, it gets a sixty degree turn toward |1⟩, and is then measured one hundred times.
